newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU approves Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.
newsitem.headline: EU approves Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger.

text.p: The European Commission recommended approval Wednesday of Boeing Co.'s planned $15 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp. after the Seattle-based aircraft maker offered last-minute concessions.
"There was a broad agreement (within the Commission). The remedies the Commission was striving for have largely been supplied," EU Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert told a news conference.

The Commission, the European Union's 20-member executive body, said it would send its recommendation -- which averts the danger of a potentially damaging transatlantic trade war -- to antitrust experts from the bloc's 15 member nations, who will review it by next week.
In Washington, the White House expressed pleasure with the outcome, which President Clinton had lobbied for this week.

"We're very pleased that the EU has recognised that Boeing went the extra mile in proposing a compromise solution and we hope that the commissioners will approve this formally when they meet next week," an administration oficial said.
Van Miert said the Commission would issue its final decision on the controversial combination next week. He added that he was confident a large majority of national experts would back the Commission.

Boeing, already the world's leading aircraft manufacturer, agreed to tone down key elements of its planned merger in order to win approval by Brussels. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has already given its go-ahead to the merger.

"By agreeing to the European Commission's conditions we took the action we believe was in the best long-term interests of our shareholders, customers, our suppliers and the more than 200,000 employees of Boeing and McDonnell Douglas," Boeing Chairman Phil Condit said in a statement issued in Brussels.
Van Miert said Boeing had accepted EU concerns about the company's long-term exclusive airplane supply contracts with three big U.S. airlines.
Boeing agreed to remove all exclusive deals from contracts with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, Continental Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc. and forego such pacts for 10 more years, he said.

Boeing had signed deals to supply its planes exclusively to the three carriers for more than 20 years, effectively snuffing out the challenge of its main rival, Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium, in large chunks of the U.S. market.
"It is a key problem. You're closing off an important part of the market," van Miert said. "This was a vital battle in terms of competition policy."
Airbus Industrie said it would not have any immediate response to the Commission's decision until it studied the details.

"Airbus Industrie takes note of the Commission's decision but has no immediate comment to make because it has no knowledge of the last minute concessions made by Boeing to counter the Commission's objections to the merger," spokesman Alain Dupeich said by telephone from Toulouse, France.
"Airbus Industrie regrets, however, the arrogant and confrontational attitude of the U.S.A. in these discussions," he added.

Boeing also agreed to free up licenses and patents from McDonnell Douglas's military research programmes to rival firms. The Commission had argued that Boeing could use government research funds, especially from the Pentagon, to subsidise its commercial aircraft development.
In another concession, the U.S. aircraft giant undertook not to abuse its dominant market position to influence the important aircraft supplies sector.
Van Miert said he was concerned that the new combined company could persuade suppliers not to cooperate with Airbus, adding that this part of the deal would be monitored closely.

The climate of negotiations as they approached a deadline had become increasingly confrontational, with Washington threatening to retaliate with possible trade sanctions if the EU Commission blocked the merger.
In Europe, French President Jacques Chirac claimed the merger was "extremely dangerous."
Europe's Airbus is operated by a consortium of French, British, German and Spanish firms.

Boeing had previously dismissed Commission fears that the merger would strengthen its already dominant position in the commercial aircraft sector, arguing that McDonnell Douglas was no longer a serious competitor.
The EU executive has the power to block major mergers if it finds they can harm fair competition in the 15-nation bloc.
In the Boeing/McDonnell Douglas case, Brussels could have levied heavy fines on the new company if it had gone ahead despite an EU ban.
